docs.title: Agentomics-ML
docs.text:
Autonomous AI agent for supervised machine learning model development on omics data

Quick Start Preprint Website

docs.title: What is Agentomics-ML?
docs.text:
Agentomics-ML is an autonomous AI agent that develops machine learning models for omics data. Given a raw dataset, it produces:

  • A trained model ready to run inference on new data
  • A detailed report summarizing the model development process and evaluation metrics

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Agentomics-ML works like an ML engineer:

  1. Explores data before designing a model
  2. Considers domain information from dataset descriptions
  3. Chooses proper data representation (encoding, normalization, feature selection)
  4. Designs and trains models, including custom neural networks
  5. Works iteratively, reacting to issues like overfitting and underfitting based on validation metrics
  6. Produces working scripts with their conda environments

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: Feature Description Any LLM Works with OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, or local models via Ollama Any Dataset Supports classification or regression datasets in CSV format Secure Execution Docker containers with read-only access to code and isolated execution Reproducible Outputs include trained models, scripts, and conda environments

docs.title: Validation Metrics
docs.text:
Available metrics for --val-metric:

Classification:

  • ACC - Accuracy
  • AUROC - Area Under ROC Curve
  • AUPRC - Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
  • F1 - F1 Score
  • PRECISION - Precision
  • RECALL - Recall
  • MCC - Matthews Correlation Coefficient
  • BALANCED_ACC - Balanced Accuracy

Regression:

  • MSE - Mean Squared Error
  • RMSE - Root Mean Squared Error
  • MAE - Mean Absolute Error
  • R2 - R-squared
  • PEARSON - Pearson Correlation

docs.title: Custom Prompts
docs.text: Customize the agent's optimization goal with custom user prompts.

docs.title: Default Prompt
docs.text:
Without customization, the agent uses:

Create the best possible machine learning model that will generalize to new unseen data.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text: ./run.sh --user-prompt "Your custom instructions here"

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simple models only: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "Only create simple ML models like logistic regression and shallow decision trees"

Focus on interpretability: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "Prioritize model interpretability over performance. Use models where feature importance can be easily explained."

Specific model type: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "Use gradient boosting models like XGBoost or LightGBM"

Handle imbalanced data: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "The dataset is highly imbalanced. Use appropriate techniques like SMOTE, class weights, or focal loss."

Neural networks: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "Focus on deep learning approaches. Design custom neural network architectures."

Quick iterations: 

./run.sh --user-prompt "Keep models simple and training fast. Avoid complex architectures that take long to train."

docs.title: What Custom Prompts Affect
docs.text:
The user prompt influences all agent steps:

Step How It's Used Data Exploration What to look for in the data Data Split Split strategy considerations Data Representation Feature encoding choices Model Architecture Model selection and design Training Training approach and hyperparameters Inference Prediction pipeline design

docs.title: Be Specific
docs.text:
Instead of:

Make a good model

Use:

Create a random forest model with feature selection. Focus on the top 50 most important features.

docs.title: Include Constraints
docs.text: Maximum training time should be 30 minutes. Model size should be under 100MB for deployment.

docs.title: Mention Domain Knowledge
docs.text: This is gene expression data. Consider using models that handle high-dimensional sparse data well.

docs.title: Specify Metrics
docs.text: Optimize for AUROC rather than accuracy, as the classes are imbalanced.

docs.title: Combining with Other Options
docs.text:
Custom prompts work with all other options:

./run.sh \
  --user-prompt "Use only sklearn models, no neural networks" \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --dataset my_data \
  --iterations 15 \
  --val-metric AUROC

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Custom prompts guide the agent but don't guarantee specific outcomes:

  • The agent may still try different approaches
  • Very restrictive prompts may limit performance
  • Some requests may not be feasible for certain datasets

docs.title: Dataset Description vs User Prompt
docs.text:
Dataset Description User Prompt Domain information about the data Instructions for the agent Goes in dataset_description.md Passed via --user-prompt Describes what the data is Describes what to do

Example dataset_description.md:

This dataset contains RNA-seq expression levels from tumor samples. Features are gene expression values.

Example user prompt:

Focus on gene signature discovery. Use feature selection to identify the most predictive genes.

Both can be used together - they complement each other.

docs.title: Advanced: Prompt Engineering
docs.text:
For complex requirements, structure your prompt:

./run.sh --user-prompt "
GOAL: Create an interpretable model for clinical use.
CONSTRAINTS:
- Must use logistic regression or decision tree
- Maximum 10 features
- Training time under 5 minutes
PRIORITIES:
1. Interpretability
2. Precision (minimize false positives)
3. Overall accuracy
"

docs.title: Multi-Architecture Builds
docs.text: For production deployments supporting both Intel/AMD and ARM processors.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Enable Docker's multi-platform builder:

# Create and use a multi-platform builder
docker buildx create --name multiplatform --use
docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

docs.title: Build Both Architectures
docs.text:
Main agent image:

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t myusername/agentomics:latest \
  --push .

Preparation image:

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -f Dockerfile.prepare \
  -t myusername/agentomics-prepare:latest \
  --push .

docs.title: With Version Tags
docs.text:
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t myusername/agentomics:v1.0 \
  -t myusername/agentomics:latest \
  --push .

docs.title: Architecture-Specific Builds
docs.text:
Build for specific architectures only:

# ARM64 only (Apple Silicon, ARM servers)
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/arm64 \
  -t myusername/agentomics:arm64 \
  --push .

# AMD64 only (Intel/AMD processors)
docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64 \
  -t myusername/agentomics:amd64 \
  --push .

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Check that images support multiple architectures:

docker buildx imagetools inspect myusername/agentomics:latest

Expected output shows both: - linux/amd64 - linux/arm64

docs.text:

docker build \
  --build-arg HTTP_PROXY=$HTTP_PROXY \
  --build-arg HTTPS_PROXY=$HTTPS_PROXY \
  --build-arg http_proxy=$http_proxy \
  --build-arg https_proxy=$https_proxy \

docs.title: GPU Settings
docs.text: Configure NVIDIA GPU support for accelerated training.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: GPU acceleration significantly speeds up: - Neural network training - Foundation model embeddings - Large dataset processing

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support
  • NVIDIA drivers installed
  • NVIDIA Container Toolkit (for Docker mode)

docs.title: Host System
docs.text:
nvidia-smi

Should show your GPU(s) with driver version and CUDA version.

docs.title: In Docker
docs.text: docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0-base nvidia-smi

docs.title: Installing NVIDIA Container Toolkit
docs.text: Follow the official guide: NVIDIA Container Toolkit Installation

docs.title: Quick Install (Ubuntu/Debian)
docs.text:
# Add repository
distribution=$(. /etc/os-release;echo $ID$VERSION_ID)
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/nvidia-docker/gpgkey | sudo apt-key add -
curl -s -L https://nvidia.github.io/nvidia-docker/$distribution/nvidia-docker.list | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nvidia-docker.list

# Install
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-container-toolkit

# Configure Docker
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0-base nvidia-smi

docs.title: Default (GPU Enabled)
docs.text:
./run.sh

GPU is detected and used automatically.

docs.title: CPU Only
docs.text:
./run.sh --cpu-only

Disables GPU even if available.

docs.title: Specific GPUs
docs.text:
Use CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES:

# Use only GPU 0
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 ./run.sh

# Use GPUs 0 and 1
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 ./run.sh

# Use no GPU (equivalent to --cpu-only)
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" ./run.sh

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
During training, monitor GPU memory:

watch -n 1 nvidia-smi

docs.title: Out of Memory
docs.text:
If you encounter OOM errors:

  1. Use --cpu-only to switch to CPU
  2. Reduce batch size in generated training scripts
  3. Use a smaller model architecture
  4. Use gradient accumulation

docs.title: Multi-GPU
docs.text:
Agentomics-ML supports multi-GPU training:

  • Agent-generated scripts may use DataParallel or DistributedDataParallel
  • All available GPUs are passed to containers by default

To limit GPUs:

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 ./run.sh  # Use only first 2 GPUs

docs.title: Docker GPU Flags
docs.text:
When running manually, use:

docker run --gpus all ...           # All GPUs
docker run --gpus '"device=0"' ...  # Specific GPU
docker run --gpus 2 ...             # First 2 GPUs

docs.title: "nvidia-smi not found"
docs.text: NVIDIA drivers not installed. Install from: NVIDIA Driver Downloads

docs.title: "docker: Error response from daemon: could not select device driver"
docs.text: NVIDIA Container Toolkit not installed or configured. Follow installation steps above.

docs.title: GPU not detected in container
docs.text:
1. Verify host GPU works: nvidia-smi
  2. Verify Docker can see GPU: docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.0-base nvidia-smi
  3. Check Docker runtime: docker info | grep -i runtime

docs.title: CUDA version mismatch
docs.text:
The container uses a specific CUDA version. If your driver is older:

  1. Update NVIDIA drivers
  2. Or use --cpu-only mode

docs.title: Performance is slow
docs.text:
• Check GPU utilization with nvidia-smi
  • Ensure you're not CPU-bound (data loading)
  • Verify training is actually using GPU (check nvidia-smi during training)

The run.sh script automatically passes proxy settings to containers.

docker run \
  -e HTTP_PROXY=$HTTP_PROXY \
  -e HTTPS_PROXY=$HTTPS_PROXY \
  -e NO_PROXY=$NO_PROXY \

docs.title: Agent Architecture
docs.text: Agentomics-ML uses a multi-step iterative architecture where each iteration refines the ML solution.

docs.title: The Iteration Loop
docs.text:
Each iteration consists of 7 sequential steps:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       ITERATION N                            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. Data Exploration    → Analyze data characteristics       │
│  2. Data Split          → Create train/validation split      │
│  3. Data Representation → Define feature encoding            │
│  4. Model Architecture  → Select and configure model         │
│  5. Training            → Train the model                    │
│  6. Inference           → Create prediction pipeline         │
│  7. Prediction Analysis → Evaluate and analyze results       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    ↓ Feedback Agent ↓                        │
│              (Guides next iteration)                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           ↓
                    ITERATION N+1

docs.title: 1. Data Exploration
docs.text:
The agent analyzes the dataset:

  • Feature distributions and statistics
  • Missing values and data quality
  • Correlations between features
  • Class balance (for classification)
  • Domain-specific insights

Output: data_exploration.json with findings

docs.title: 2. Data Split
docs.text:
Creates or modifies train/validation split:

  • Stratified splitting for classification
  • Considers data distribution
  • May adjust split based on previous iterations

Output: data_split.json with split info

Note

The agent can modify splits during early iterations (controlled by --split-allowed-iterations).

docs.title: 3. Data Representation
docs.text:
Defines how data is encoded:

  • Numeric normalization/standardization
  • Categorical encoding (one-hot, label encoding)
  • Feature selection
  • Custom transformations for omics data

Output: data_representation.json with encoding scheme

docs.title: 4. Model Architecture
docs.text:
Selects and configures the model:

  • Model type (sklearn, neural network, etc.)
  • Hyperparameters
  • Architecture details for neural networks
  • Regularization strategies

Output: model_architecture.json with configuration

docs.title: 5. Training
docs.text:
Implements and runs training:

  • Generates train.py script
  • Sets up conda environment
  • Executes training
  • Monitors for issues (overfitting, convergence)

Output: train.py and training artifacts

docs.title: 6. Inference
docs.text:
Creates prediction pipeline:

  • Generates inference.py script
  • Ensures reproducibility
  • Handles data preprocessing
  • Validates predictions

Output: inference.py script

docs.title: 7. Prediction Analysis
docs.text:
Evaluates model performance:

  • Calculates validation metrics
  • Analyzes prediction distributions
  • Identifies potential issues
  • Compares to previous iterations

Output: Metrics and analysis

docs.title: Agent Tools
docs.text:
The agent has access to these tools:

Tool Purpose Bash Execute shell commands Write Python Create Python files Run Python Execute Python scripts Replace Modify code sections Foundation Models Info Get domain model information

docs.title: How Decisions Are Made
docs.text:
Each step uses an LLM agent that:

  1. Receives context (data info, previous results, feedback)
  2. Generates a structured output (validated by Pydantic)
  3. Validates the output meets requirements
  4. Retries if validation fails (up to 10 times)

docs.title: Iteration Flow
docs.text:
Iteration 0 (Baseline)
├── Full exploration
├── Initial split
├── Basic representation
├── Simple model
└── Baseline metrics

Iteration 1-N (Refinement)
├── Focused exploration (guided by feedback)
├── Split adjustment (if allowed)
├── Improved representation
├── Better model/hyperparameters
└── Compare to best so far

Final
├── Select best iteration
├── Evaluate on test set
└── Generate reports

docs.title: Snapshot System
docs.text:
The agent tracks the best-performing iteration:

  • After each iteration, metrics are compared
  • If better than previous best, a snapshot is saved
  • Snapshots include model, scripts, and environment
  • Final evaluation uses the best snapshot

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Key architecture parameters in src/utils/config.py:

Parameter Default Description temperature 1.0 LLM creativity level max_steps 100 Max steps per agent max_validation_retries 10 Output validation retries llm_response_timeout 900s LLM response timeout bash_tool_timeout 300s Bash command timeout run_python_tool_timeout 21600s Training timeout (6 hours)

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: How Agentomics-ML evaluates model performance.

docs.title: Evaluation Stages
docs.text:
Models are evaluated at multiple stages:

Stage Data Used Purpose Dry Run Small sample Validate inference script works Validation Validation set Guide optimization Train Training set Detect overfitting Test Hidden test set Final unbiased evaluation

docs.title: Validation Evaluation
docs.text:
After each iteration:

  1. Model makes predictions on validation set
  2. Metrics calculated based on task type
  3. Compared to previous iterations
  4. Best iteration snapshot updated if improved

docs.title: Test Evaluation
docs.text:
At the end of the run:

  1. Best iteration's model is loaded
  2. Predictions made on test set (never seen during training)
  3. Final metrics reported
  4. Results saved to final report

Note

Test evaluation only occurs if you provide a test.csv file.

docs.title: Classification Metrics
docs.text: Metric Code Description Accuracy ACC Correct predictions / Total predictions AUROC AUROC Area Under ROC Curve AUPRC AUPRC Area Under Precision-Recall Curve F1 Score F1 Harmonic mean of precision and recall Precision PRECISION True positives / Predicted positives Recall RECALL True positives / Actual positives MCC MCC Matthews Correlation Coefficient Balanced Accuracy BALANCED_ACC Average recall per class

docs.title: When to Use Each
docs.text: Metric Best For ACC Balanced classes, general performance AUROC Comparing models, imbalanced data AUPRC Highly imbalanced data F1 Balance of precision and recall PRECISION Minimizing false positives RECALL Minimizing false negatives MCC Imbalanced data, overall quality

docs.title: Regression Metrics
docs.text: Metric Code Description Mean Squared Error MSE Average squared difference Root MSE RMSE Square root of MSE Mean Absolute Error MAE Average absolute difference R-squared R2 Proportion of variance explained Pearson Correlation PEARSON Linear correlation coefficient

docs.title: When to Use Each
docs.text: Metric Best For MSE/RMSE Penalizing large errors MAE Robust to outliers R2 Understanding explained variance PEARSON Linear relationship strength

docs.title: Selecting Validation Metric
docs.text:
Choose with --val-metric:

./run.sh --val-metric AUROC

The agent optimizes for this metric when selecting the best iteration.

docs.title: Metric Calculation
docs.text:
Metrics are calculated using scikit-learn:

from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, f1_score

# Classification
accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
auroc = roc_auc_score(y_true, y_proba)
f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')

# Regression
mse = mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)
r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)

docs.title: Multi-class Handling
docs.text:
For multi-class classification:

  • AUROC: One-vs-rest, macro average
  • F1: Weighted average by class support
  • Precision/Recall: Macro or weighted average

docs.title: Overfitting Detection
docs.text:
The agent monitors for overfitting by comparing:

  • Training metrics vs. validation metrics
  • Large gaps indicate overfitting

Example feedback when overfitting detected:

Train ACC: 0.98, Validation ACC: 0.72 Significant overfitting detected. Consider regularization.

docs.title: Best Iteration Selection
docs.text:
The best iteration is selected by:

  1. Comparing validation metric across all iterations
  2. Higher is better for most metrics (ACC, AUROC, F1, R2)
  3. Lower is better for error metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE)

docs.title: During Run
docs.text:
Progress shows current metrics:

Iteration 5: Validation ACC = 0.847 (Best: 0.852 at iter 3)

docs.title: In Reports
docs.text:
reports/final_report.txt

Contains: - All iteration metrics - Best iteration details - Test set results - Metric comparisons

docs.title: In W&B
docs.text:
If configured, metrics are logged to Weights & Biases:

  • Metric plots over iterations
  • Comparison tables
  • Artifact tracking

docs.title: Custom Evaluation
docs.text:
For advanced use, modify evaluation in:

src/eval/metrics_calculator.py

Add custom metrics or modify calculation behavior.

docs.title: Feedback Loop
docs.text: The feedback agent guides improvements between iterations.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
After each iteration completes:

  1. Results Collected - Metrics, model outputs, and analysis from all steps
  2. Feedback Generated - A separate LLM analyzes what worked and what didn't
  3. Instructions Created - Specific guidance for each step in the next iteration
  4. Next Iteration Starts - Agents receive feedback as part of their context

docs.title: Feedback Structure
docs.text:
The feedback agent produces instructions for each step:

IterationInstructions
├── data_exploration_instructions
├── data_split_instructions
├── data_representation_instructions
├── model_architecture_instructions
├── model_training_instructions
├── inference_instructions
├── prediction_exploration_instructions
└── other_instructions

docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text:
• Current vs. previous validation metrics
  • Best iteration so far
  • Metric trends across iterations

docs.title: Issues Detected
docs.text:
• Overfitting (train >> validation performance)
  • Underfitting (poor performance on both)
  • Class imbalance effects
  • Feature problems

docs.title: Model Behavior
docs.text:
• Training convergence
  • Prediction distribution
  • Error patterns

docs.title: Time Constraints
docs.text:
• Remaining time (if timeout set)
  • Training duration of previous models

docs.title: Overfitting Detected
docs.text: Model Architecture Instructions: The previous model overfit significantly (train ACC 0.98, val ACC 0.72). Try stronger regularization: increase dropout to 0.5, add L2 regularization, or use a simpler architecture with fewer layers.

docs.title: Underfitting Detected
docs.text: Model Architecture Instructions: The model underfits (train ACC 0.65, val ACC 0.63). Consider a more complex model: deeper network, more trees, or additional features in the representation.

docs.title: Good Progress
docs.text: Model Training Instructions: Good improvement from 0.75 to 0.82 AUROC. Continue with similar architecture but try fine-tuning learning rate (try 1e-4) and increasing epochs.

docs.title: Exploration vs. Optimization
docs.text: The feedback agent manages two phases:

docs.title: Exploration Phase
docs.text:
Early iterations (controlled by --exploration-iterations):

  • Try diverse approaches
  • Test different model types
  • Explore data representations
  • Build baseline understanding

docs.title: Optimization Phase
docs.text:
Later iterations:

  • Focus on best-performing approaches
  • Fine-tune hyperparameters
  • Improve on winning strategy
  • Polish the solution

docs.title: Combination Tracking
docs.text:
The feedback agent tracks which combinations have been tried:

Representation × Architecture Combinations:
✓ StandardScaler + LogisticRegression → 0.72 ACC
✓ StandardScaler + RandomForest → 0.78 ACC
✓ PCA + RandomForest → 0.75 ACC
✗ MinMaxScaler + GradientBoosting → Not tried yet

This prevents repeating failed approaches and encourages exploration.

docs.title: Split Management
docs.text:
For early iterations, the agent may suggest split changes:

Data Split Instructions: Validation set may be too small for reliable metrics. Consider increasing validation size to 30% for better estimates.

After --split-allowed-iterations, splits are frozen to ensure fair comparison.

docs.title: Feedback Agent Model
docs.text:
By default, the feedback agent uses the same LLM as the main agent. You can specify a different model:

  • Main agent: Complex reasoning for code generation
  • Feedback agent: Can be faster/cheaper for analysis

docs.title: Viewing Feedback
docs.text:
Feedback is included in iteration reports:

reports/run_report_iter_N.txt

Each report shows: - What feedback was received - How the agent responded - Results of the iteration

docs.text: Parameter Default Description --exploration-iterations 3 Iterations for broad exploration --split-allowed-iterations 3 Iterations that can modify splits

docs.title: Batch Experiments
docs.text: Run multiple experiments across models and datasets with orchestrator.sh.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The orchestrator script automates running Agentomics-ML across:

  • Multiple LLM models
  • Multiple datasets
  • Consistent configuration

Useful for: - Benchmarking different models - Testing across datasets - Systematic experiments

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
./orchestrator.sh

The script reads configuration and runs experiments in sequence.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Edit orchestrator.sh to configure:

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
MODELS=(
    "openai/gpt-4o"
    "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet"
    "openai/gpt-4-turbo"
)

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
DATASETS=(
    "breast_cancer"
    "gene_expression"
    "protein_classification"
)

docs.title: Common Parameters
docs.text:
ITERATIONS=10
VAL_METRIC="AUROC"
TIMEOUT=7200

docs.title: Experiment Matrix
docs.text:
The orchestrator runs all combinations:

Model 1 × Dataset 1 → Run 1
Model 1 × Dataset 2 → Run 2
Model 1 × Dataset 3 → Run 3
Model 2 × Dataset 1 → Run 4
...

docs.title: Output Organization
docs.text:
Results are organized by model and dataset:

outputs/
├── gpt-4o_breast_cancer_<timestamp>/
├── gpt-4o_gene_expression_<timestamp>/
├── claude-3.5-sonnet_breast_cancer_<timestamp>/
└── ...

docs.title: Spend Limits
docs.text:
Set maximum API spend:

MAX_SPEND=100.00  # USD

Experiments stop if spend limit is reached (OpenRouter only).

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Add tags for experiment tracking:

TAGS="benchmark-v1,paper-experiments"

Tags appear in W&B if logging is enabled.

docs.title: Timeout per Run
docs.text:
Set maximum time per experiment:

TIMEOUT=7200  # 2 hours per run

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash

# Models to test
MODELS=(
    "openai/gpt-4o"
    "anthropic/claude-3.5-sonnet"
)

# Datasets to use
DATASETS=(
    "dataset_a"
    "dataset_b"
)

# Run parameters
ITERATIONS=10
VAL_METRIC="AUROC"
TIMEOUT=3600

# Limits
MAX_SPEND=50.00

# Run all combinations
for model in "${MODELS[@]}"; do
    for dataset in "${DATASETS[@]}"; do
        ./run.sh \
            --model "$model" \
            --dataset "$dataset" \
            --iterations "$ITERATIONS" \
            --val-metric "$VAL_METRIC" \
            --timeout "$TIMEOUT"
    done
done

docs.title: Parallel Execution
docs.text:
For parallel runs on multiple machines:

  1. Split the model/dataset combinations
  2. Run different subsets on each machine
  3. Combine results afterward

docs.title: Progress
docs.text:
Each run outputs progress to console:

[1/6] Running: gpt-4o on breast_cancer
[2/6] Running: gpt-4o on gene_expression
...

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
If W&B is configured, all runs are tracked:

  • Compare runs in W&B dashboard
  • Filter by tags
  • Analyze trends

docs.title: Single Run Failure
docs.text: If one run fails, the orchestrator continues with the next combination.

docs.title: Retry Failed Runs
docs.text:
Re-run only failed experiments:

./orchestrator.sh --retry-failed

docs.title: Skip Completed
docs.text:
Skip already-completed runs:

./orchestrator.sh --skip-completed

docs.title: BioMLBench Integration
docs.text:
For benchmark datasets:

./orchestrator.sh --biomlbench

Uses the BioMLBench dataset collection for standardized evaluation.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Start Small - Test with 1 model, 1 dataset first
  2. Set Timeouts - Prevent runaway experiments
  3. Use Tags - Track experiment versions
  4. Enable Logging - Use W&B for comparison
  5. Monitor Spend - Set spend limits for paid APIs

docs.title: Foundation Models
docs.text: Pre-trained models for specialized omics domains.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Foundation models are large pre-trained models specialized for specific data types. Agentomics-ML can pre-download these models to speed up agent runs.

docs.title: Available Types
docs.text: Type Domain Use Case dna Genomics DNA sequences, variants rna Transcriptomics RNA sequences, expression protein Proteomics Protein sequences, structure molecule Chemistry Small molecules, drugs

docs.title: Pre-downloading Models
docs.text:
Download foundation models before running:

./run.sh --foundation-model-type dna

This downloads relevant models to the Docker image, avoiding download delays during agent execution.

docs.title: Multiple Types
docs.text:
Download multiple types by running multiple times:

./run.sh --foundation-model-type dna
./run.sh --foundation-model-type protein

docs.title: DNA Models
docs.text:
For genomic sequence data:

  • Variant effect prediction
  • Regulatory element detection
  • Sequence classification

Example datasets: - Gene expression from DNA features - SNP effect prediction - Promoter classification

docs.title: RNA Models
docs.text:
For transcriptomic data:

  • RNA sequence analysis
  • Secondary structure prediction
  • Expression-based classification

Example datasets: - RNA-seq classification - Splice site prediction - RNA modification detection

docs.title: Protein Models
docs.text:
For protein sequence data:

  • Protein function prediction
  • Structure-based classification
  • Interaction prediction

Example datasets: - Protein family classification - Enzyme activity prediction - Binding site detection

docs.title: Molecule Models
docs.text:
For small molecule/chemical data:

  • Drug property prediction
  • Molecular classification
  • Activity prediction

Example datasets: - Drug-target interaction - Toxicity prediction - ADMET properties

docs.title: How the Agent Uses Foundation Models
docs.text:
1. Discovery - Agent queries available foundation models
  2. Selection - Agent chooses appropriate model for the data
  3. Embedding - Features extracted using the model
  4. Training - Embeddings used as input to ML model

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Foundation model configurations are in:

foundation_models/

Each type has a configuration specifying: - Model names and sources - Download locations - Usage instructions for the agent

docs.title: Without Pre-downloading
docs.text: If you don't pre-download, the agent can still use foundation models but will download them during execution (slower first run).

docs.title: Storage Requirements
docs.text:
Foundation models can be large:

Type Approximate Size DNA 1-5 GB RNA 1-5 GB Protein 2-10 GB Molecule 0.5-2 GB

Ensure sufficient disk space in the Docker volume or local environment.

docs.title: GPU Acceleration
docs.text:
Foundation models benefit significantly from GPU:

  • With GPU: Fast embedding generation
  • CPU only: Much slower, but functional

Use --cpu-only if GPU unavailable, but expect longer run times for foundation model-based approaches.

docs.title: Custom Foundation Models
docs.text:
To add custom foundation models:

  1. Add configuration to foundation_models/
  2. Update the download script
  3. Add usage instructions for the agent

docs.title: Metrics Reference
docs.text: Complete list of available metrics for model evaluation.

docs.title: Accuracy (ACC)
docs.text:
The proportion of correct predictions.

ACC = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Balanced datasets

docs.title: AUROC
docs.text:
Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve.

Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Ranking quality, imbalanced data

Multi-class: Uses one-vs-rest with macro averaging.

docs.title: AUPRC
docs.text:
Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve.

Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Highly imbalanced data

Better than AUROC when positive class is rare.

docs.title: F1 Score (F1)
docs.text:
Harmonic mean of precision and recall.

F1 = 2 * (Precision * Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Balance precision and recall

Multi-class: Uses weighted averaging by default.

docs.title: Precision (PRECISION)
docs.text:
Proportion of positive predictions that are correct.

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)
Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Minimize false positives

docs.title: Recall (RECALL)
docs.text:
Proportion of actual positives that are correctly identified.

Recall = TP / (TP + FN)
Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Minimize false negatives

docs.title: Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)
docs.text:
Correlation between predicted and actual classifications.

Property Value Range -1 to 1 Best Higher (1 is perfect) Use case Imbalanced data, overall quality

Considered one of the best single metrics for binary classification.

docs.title: Balanced Accuracy (BALANCED_ACC)
docs.text:
Average recall across all classes.

Property Value Range 0 to 1 Best Higher Use case Multi-class with imbalance

docs.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
docs.text:
Average of squared prediction errors.

MSE = (1/n) * Σ(y_true - y_pred)²
Property Value Range 0 to ∞ Best Lower Use case Penalizing large errors

docs.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
docs.text:
Square root of MSE.

RMSE = √MSE
Property Value Range 0 to ∞ Best Lower Use case Same units as target

docs.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
docs.text:
Average of absolute prediction errors.

MAE = (1/n) * Σ|y_true - y_pred|
Property Value Range 0 to ∞ Best Lower Use case Robust to outliers

docs.title: R-squared (R2)
docs.text:
Proportion of variance explained by the model.

R² = 1 - (SS_res / SS_tot)
Property Value Range -∞ to 1 Best Higher (1 is perfect) Use case Model explanatory power

Can be negative if model is worse than predicting the mean.

docs.title: Pearson Correlation (PEARSON)
docs.text:
Linear correlation between predictions and true values.

Property Value Range -1 to 1 Best Higher absolute value Use case Linear relationship strength

docs.text: Scenario Recommended Metric Balanced classes ACC, F1 Imbalanced classes AUROC, AUPRC, MCC Minimize false positives PRECISION Minimize false negatives RECALL Overall quality MCC Model ranking AUROC

docs.title: Regression
docs.text: Scenario Recommended Metric General performance RMSE, R2 Outlier-robust MAE Relative performance R2, PEARSON Same units as target RMSE, MAE

docs.title: Preparing Datasets
docs.text: Agentomics-ML works with CSV datasets for classification or regression tasks.

docs.title: Quick Setup
docs.text:
Create a folder in datasets/ with your data:

datasets/my_dataset/
├── train.csv              # Required
├── validation.csv         # Optional
├── test.csv               # Optional
└── dataset_description.md # Optional

docs.title: train.csv (Required)
docs.text:
Your training data with features and a target column.

feature1,feature2,feature3,target
1.2,3.4,5.6,positive
7.8,9.0,1.2,negative

docs.title: validation.csv (Optional)
docs.text: Separate validation data. If not provided, the agent creates a train/validation split from train.csv.

docs.title: test.csv (Optional)
docs.text: Hidden test set for final evaluation. The agent never sees this data during training - it's only used to report final metrics.

docs.title: dataset_description.md (Optional)
docs.text:
Domain information to help the agent understand your data:

# Gene Expression Dataset

This dataset contains RNA-seq expression levels from tumor samples.

## Features
- Columns 1-100: Gene expression values (log2 TPM)
- Samples are from breast cancer patients

## Target
- `class`: tumor subtype (Basal, Her2, LumA, LumB, Normal)

## Notes
- Data is already normalized
- Consider using models that handle high-dimensional data

docs.title: Target Column Detection
docs.text:
The agent auto-detects the target column from common names:

  • class
  • target
  • label
  • y

If auto-detection fails, you'll be prompted to select the target column during preparation.

docs.title: Manual Dataset Preparation
docs.text:
For more control, run preparation separately:

# Create preparation environment
conda env create -f environment_prepare.yaml
conda activate agentomics-prepare-env

# Prepare datasets
python src/prepare_datasets.py

docs.title: Preparation Options
docs.text:
python src/prepare_datasets.py --help

Key options:

Option Description --dataset-dir Specific dataset to prepare --task-type Force classification or regression --target-column Specify target column name --positive-class Define positive class for binary classification

docs.title: Prepared Dataset Structure
docs.text:
After preparation, datasets are stored in:

prepared_datasets/my_dataset/
├── train.csv              # Training data
├── validation.csv         # Validation data (created if not provided)
├── train.no_label.csv     # Training data without labels (for inference)
├── validation.no_label.csv
└── metadata.json          # Task type, classes, etc.

prepared_test_sets/my_dataset/
├── test.csv               # Test data (if provided)
└── test.no_label.csv

docs.title: Example Datasets
docs.text:
Download example datasets:

conda env create -f competitors/environment_datasets.yaml
conda activate agentomics-datasets
python src/utils/create_datasets.py
conda deactivate

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
• Target column should contain class labels (strings or integers)
  • Binary: positive/negative, 1/0, yes/no
  • Multi-class: class_a, class_b, class_c

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
• Target column should contain numeric values
  • The agent auto-detects regression when target is continuous

docs.title: Feature Columns
docs.text:
• Numeric features work best
  • Categorical features are supported (encoded automatically)
  • Missing values are handled, but clean data performs better

docs.title: "Could not detect target column"
docs.text: Solution: Add --target-column your_column_name to preparation command, or rename your target column to class, target, label, or y.

docs.title: "Task type unclear"
docs.text: Solution: Add --task-type classification or --task-type regression to force the task type.

docs.title: Running Inference
docs.text: Use trained models to make predictions on new data with inference.sh.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
./inference.sh \
  --agent-dir outputs/<agent_id> \
  --input /path/to/new_data.csv \
  --output /path/to/predictions.csv

docs.title: Required Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description --agent-dir Path to completed agent output folder --input Path to input CSV file (without labels) --output Path where predictions will be saved

docs.title: Optional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description --cpu-only Run without GPU --local Run locally without Docker --help Show help message

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
./inference.sh \
  --agent-dir outputs/enchanted_fixing_reigned \
  --input new_samples.csv \
  --output predictions.csv

docs.title: Input Data Format
docs.text:
Your input file should:

  • Be a CSV file
  • Have the same feature columns as training data
  • Not include the target/label column

Example: 

feature1,feature2,feature3
1.2,3.4,5.6
7.8,9.0,1.2

docs.title: Output Format
docs.text:
Predictions are saved as a CSV with a single column:

predictions
positive
negative
positive

The order matches your input data rows.

docs.title: Docker vs Local Mode
docs.text:
# Docker mode (default, recommended)
./inference.sh --agent-dir outputs/my_agent ...

# Local mode
./inference.sh --local --agent-dir outputs/my_agent ...

docs.title: GPU Support
docs.text:
GPU is used automatically if available:

# Use GPU (default)
./inference.sh --agent-dir outputs/my_agent ...

# CPU only
./inference.sh --cpu-only --agent-dir outputs/my_agent ...

docs.title: Using the Inference Script Directly
docs.text:
For more control, use the agent's inference script directly:

# Navigate to agent's best run
cd outputs/<agent_id>/best_run_files

# Activate the environment
conda activate .conda/envs/<agent_id>_env

# Run inference
python inference.py --input /path/to/data.csv --output /path/to/predictions.csv

docs.title: What's in best_run_files
docs.text:
outputs/<agent_id>/best_run_files/
├── inference.py           # Inference script
├── train.py               # Training script
├── model.joblib           # Trained model (or other format)
├── .conda/                # Conda environment
└── ...                    # Other artifacts (tokenizers, etc.)

docs.title: "Docker image not found"
docs.text: Run ./run.sh once to build the Docker image, or use --local mode.

docs.title: "Column mismatch"
docs.text: Ensure your input CSV has the same feature columns as the training data (minus the target column).

docs.title: "Model file not found"
docs.text: Check that best_run_files/ contains the model artifacts. If the agent run failed, there may be no trained model.

docs.title: GPU out of memory
docs.text: Use --cpu-only flag or reduce batch size in the inference script.

docs.title: Batch Inference
docs.text: For large datasets, the inference script handles batching automatically. If you need custom batch sizes, modify the inference.py script in best_run_files/.

docs.title: Running the Agent
docs.text: The main entry point for Agentomics-ML is run.sh. This guide covers both interactive and non-interactive usage.

docs.title: Interactive Mode
docs.text:
Running without arguments launches interactive mode:

./run.sh

You'll be prompted to select:

  1. LLM Model - Choose from available models
  2. Dataset - Select a prepared dataset
  3. Iterations - Number of optimization cycles (default: 10)
  4. Validation Metric - Metric to optimize (ACC, AUROC, etc.)

docs.title: Non-Interactive Mode
docs.text:
Supply parameters directly to skip prompts:

./run.sh \
  --model openai/gpt-4o \
  --dataset breast_cancer \
  --iterations 10 \
  --val-metric ACC

docs.title: Common Options
docs.text: Option Description Example --model LLM model to use --model openai/gpt-4o --dataset Dataset name --dataset my_data --iterations Number of iterations --iterations 15 --val-metric Validation metric --val-metric AUROC --timeout Time limit in seconds --timeout 3600

docs.title: Listing Available Options
docs.text:
# List available models
./run.sh --list-models

# List prepared datasets
./run.sh --list-datasets

# List available metrics
./run.sh --list-metrics

docs.text: Flag Description --pull-images Pull pre-built Docker images --local Run without Docker (uses conda) --cpu-only Disable GPU acceleration --ollama Use local Ollama models

docs.text:
Pre-download domain-specific foundation models:

./run.sh --foundation-model-type dna

Available types: dna, rna, protein, molecule

docs.title: Time Limits
docs.text:
Set a deadline for the entire run:

./run.sh --timeout 7200  # 2 hour limit

docs.title: Custom User Prompt
docs.text:
Override the default optimization goal:

./run.sh --user-prompt "Only use simple models like logistic regression"

See Custom Prompts for more details.

docs.title: What Happens During a Run
docs.text:
1. Dataset Preparation - Validates and prepares data in prepared_datasets/
  2. Iterative Development - Agent runs exploration, training, and evaluation cycles
  3. Snapshot Best Model - Tracks the best-performing iteration
  4. Final Evaluation - Tests on held-out test set (if provided)
  5. Output Results - Saves everything to outputs/<agent_id>/

docs.title: Monitoring Progress
docs.text:
During execution, you'll see:

  • Current iteration number
  • Agent step (exploration, training, etc.)
  • Validation metrics after each iteration
  • Best iteration tracking

docs.title: Re-training Models
docs.text: After the agent completes a run, you can re-train the model with new data using the train.sh script.

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text:
• Train on updated or expanded datasets
  • Fine-tune with additional samples
  • Reproduce training with different data splits

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
./train.sh \
  --agent-dir outputs/<agent_id> \
  --train-data /path/to/new_train.csv \
  --validation-data /path/to/new_validation.csv \
  --artifacts-dir /path/to/output_artifacts

docs.title: Required Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description --agent-dir Path to completed agent output folder --train-data Path to new training CSV file --validation-data Path to new validation CSV file --artifacts-dir Where to save new training artifacts

docs.title: Optional Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description --cpu-only Run without GPU --local Run locally without Docker --help Show help message

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Re-train using new data
./train.sh \
  --agent-dir outputs/enchanted_fixing_reigned \
  --train-data datasets/updated_data/train.csv \
  --validation-data datasets/updated_data/validation.csv \
  --artifacts-dir outputs/retrained_model

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The script:

  1. Loads the agent's train.py script from best_run_files/
  2. Uses the agent's conda environment
  3. Runs training with the new data
  4. Saves artifacts to the specified directory

docs.title: Data Format
docs.text:
Your new data files must match the format expected by the agent's training script:

  • Same column names as original training data
  • Same feature encoding/preprocessing expectations
  • Target column with same name and format

./train.sh --local --agent-dir outputs/my_agent ...
